clinicalPearls: Results from ingestion of Aconitum species (monkshood, wolfsbane), often through herbal or traditional medicine preparations, contaminated foraged roots, or accidental use of the ornamental plant.
Aconitine and related diterpenoid alkaloids bind open voltage-gated sodium channels, causing persistent depolarisation of cardiac, neuronal and muscle membranes.
The combination of early paraesthesiae and numbness (perioral then generalised) with gastrointestinal upset followed by life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia is highly suggestive.
Refractory ventricular tachyarrhythmias, including bidirectional ventricular tachycardia, are the hallmark and principal cause of death.
Neuromuscular features include weakness, and severe cases may develop respiratory muscle involvement and hypotension from the same channel effect.

There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with continuous cardiac monitoring, antiarrhythmic drugs such as amiodarone, and consideration of cardiopulmonary bypass or extracorporeal support for refractory arrhythmia.
Toxin content varies greatly between plant parts, species and processing, so poisoning can occur even from products believed to be therapeutic doses of herbal medicine.
The alkaloids can be absorbed through mucosa and skin, and there is no safe reliable domestic method to detoxify the raw plant.
reference.pathophysiology: Aconite poisoning is caused by aconitine and structurally related diterpenoid ester alkaloids concentrated in the roots and other parts of Aconitum plants. These alkaloids bind with high affinity to the open state of voltage-gated sodium channels at neuronal, cardiac and skeletal-muscle sites, preventing channel inactivation. Sodium channels therefore remain persistently open, causing sustained membrane depolarisation and increased cellular excitability. In the myocardium this produces enhanced automaticity, triggered activity and re-entry, generating the characteristic and often refractory ventricular tachyarrhythmias including bidirectional ventricular tachycardia; vagal stimulation and direct effects also cause bradyarrhythmias and hypotension. In peripheral and autonomic nerves the same mechanism produces the early paraesthesiae, numbness and later weakness, along with nausea, vomiting, salivation and diaphoresis. Persistent activation eventually leads to a depolarising conduction block that can affect respiratory muscles. The toxins are rapidly absorbed across the gastrointestinal and other mucosae and even through intact skin, and their potency together with wide variation in plant and preparation content accounts for the narrow margin between traditional therapeutic use and severe poisoning.
additionalDifferentials: Digoxin or cardiac glycoside (including oleander) toxicity
Other sodium-channel-active drug toxicity such as class I antiarrhythmics or local anaesthetics
Ciguatera fish poisoning with paraesthesiae and bradycardia
Primary cardiac cause of ventricular arrhythmia
Electrolyte disturbance provoking arrhythmia, such as hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia
additionalInvestigations: Continuous electrocardiographic monitoring and serial 12-lead ECGs to detect ventricular and bidirectional tachycardia
Serum electrolytes including potassium and magnesium to correct arrhythmogenic disturbance
Renal function and acid-base status in shocked or arrhythmic patients
Detection of aconitine alkaloids in blood or urine at a specialist laboratory where available
Digoxin level or cardiac glycoside assay to help exclude glycoside toxicity
Cardiac biomarkers if myocardial injury is suspected
Identification of the plant or herbal preparation ingested
redFlags: Ventricular arrhythmia or bidirectional ventricular tachycardia on the monitor
Hypotension or signs of cardiogenic shock
Respiratory muscle weakness or failing ventilation
reference.prognosis: Mild poisoning with only sensory and gastrointestinal symptoms usually resolves with supportive care, but severe poisoning with refractory ventricular arrhythmia carries a high mortality. Survival is improved by early continuous cardiac monitoring and, in refractory cases, extracorporeal circulatory support.
pitfalls: Assuming a herbal or traditional preparation is inherently safe and overlooking aconite as the cause
Failing to institute continuous cardiac monitoring in a patient with only early paraesthesiae
Treating arrhythmia as a primary cardiac event without seeking the toxicological history
Underestimating dermal and mucosal absorption as routes of exposure
Delaying escalation to extracorporeal support in refractory ventricular arrhythmia
references: Herbal and plant poisoning reference materials
Emergency medicine and cardiology reference texts
management: No specific antidote exists, so immediate continuous cardiac monitoring and supportive resuscitation take priority
Antiarrhythmic therapy for the characteristic ventricular tachyarrhythmias, with amiodarone (or lidocaine or flecainide) and electrical cardioversion for unstable rhythm
Correct potassium and magnesium, treat hypotension with fluids and vasopressors, and manage bradyarrhythmia with atropine
Consider gastrointestinal decontamination with activated charcoal after early presentation following a significant ingestion
Extracorporeal life support such as venoarterial ECMO or cardiopulmonary bypass for refractory arrhythmia or shock as a bridge to recovery
Supportive respiratory care including mechanical ventilation if respiratory muscle weakness develops
Identify the source such as herbal or traditional-medicine preparations or foraged Aconitum and involve poisons and toxicology services
